CC before i = a long "ch": doc-cia. SC before e = "sh": pesce = "pe-she".
UO is said together, as a diphthong: UO-va. Likewise: buono, nuovo, uomo.
The pronoun attaches to the verb in pronunciation: mi-SVE-lyo, ti-AL-tsi, si-VE-ste.
1. Reflexive verbs: just like in Romanian!
Reflexive verbs have "-si" in the infinitive: alzarsi, svegliarsi, vestirsi. As in Romanian ("a se scula"), the reflexive pronoun goes before the conjugated verb.
They're conjugated like normal verbs (alzare → alzo, alzi, alza…), you just add the pronoun. "Vestirsi" is an -ire verb: mi vesto, ti vesti, si veste.
2. Verbs reflexive in Italian but not in Romanian (and vice versa)
After "devo, voglio, posso", the pronoun attaches to the infinitive (which drops its -e):
Tomorrow I have to get up at six.
Do you want to rest a bit?
It can also go before: "Domani mi devo alzare alle sei." Both are correct.
"Never" has two parts, as in Romanian ("nu… niciodată"): "non" before the verb, "mai" after it. "Non bevo mai il latte." If "mai" comes first, there's no "non": "Mai prima dell'una."
5. The order of actions and the right time
Connectors for telling a day: prima (first), poi (then), dopo (afterwards), più tardi (later), alla fine (in the end).
"Presto" also means "soon": "A presto!" = "See you soon!". And "Sono in ritardo" = "I'm late", in the sense of delayed.

Graziella wakes up every morning at half past five, without an alarm clock. She gets up straight away, washes, gets dressed and combs her hair in front of her grandmother's mirror.
At six she goes down to the trattoria. First she makes the coffee, then she prepares the sauce for lunch. The sauce has to simmer for three hours: there's no hurry.
At half past seven Pietro arrives with his books. He has breakfast with his grandmother: milk, bread and jam. Then he goes to school, always running.
From twelve to three the trattoria is full. Graziella never sits down. After lunch she rests for half an hour in the chair by the window, with Michelangelo on her lap.
In the evening she works again until half past ten. Often, at the end, she has dinner with Matei, who always arrives at the last minute.
At midnight she goes to bed. But before falling asleep she always reads two pages of a book of poems.
Once Matei asks her: "Graziella, when do you really rest?" She laughs: "I rest when everyone has eaten well, dear."
